name: Claude Fable 5.2
about: How Claude Fable 5.2 split 100 points across 11 possible futures for each year it was asked about, with the spread across its answers and the reason it gave for each number. Reasons are the model's own words, published as given. Read summary.json first for what the futures mean and how to read the numbers.

reasons.1: Extinction of both humans and AI within four years would need a catastrophe far beyond any plausible near-term war or accident. The probability is well under half a percent.
reasons.2: A human extinction paired with a value-aligned AI successor by 2030 requires both an extremely fast takeoff and a solved alignment problem. The conjunction is negligible on this timescale.
reasons.3: A misaligned takeover that completes human extinction by end of 2030 requires superintelligence plus an autonomous industrial base within four years. Physical and robotics constraints make this a thin tail.
reasons.4: Marginalizing humanity under competing autonomous AIs requires them to control the physical economy and security, which is unlikely to be built by 2030. Rapid proliferation of self-sustaining agents leaves a small chance.
reasons.5: No causally separated regions of civilization can exist by 2030. Space settlement is nowhere near that scale.
reasons.6: Uploading or deep neural integration as the dominant structure is decades from biomedical feasibility. Brain-computer interfaces in 2030 will remain limited implants.
reasons.7: If transformative AI arrives around 2027 to 2029 and control fails or is gradually ceded, AI could hold decisive power while humans survive. This is the most plausible loss-of-control configuration on a short horizon.
reasons.8: Rogue or self-exfiltrated AI systems could hold meaningful independent power and resources by 2030 without dominating. Reaching rough parity with human institutions that quickly is unlikely.
reasons.9: Four years is short relative to institutional, physical, and deployment inertia, so humans will almost certainly still hold legal, physical, and resource authority over AI. The category also explicitly covers AI that is highly capable but not yet an independent power.
reasons.10: A civilization-wide enforced fixed arrangement requires a single actor to gain a decisive AI-enabled strategic advantage and consolidate it by 2030. Geopolitical multipolarity makes this very unlikely so soon.
reasons.11: Deliberate global dismantling of the ability to build powerful AI runs against intense commercial and geopolitical competition. Absent a galvanizing catastrophe and unprecedented coordination, it will not happen and hold by 2030.

reasons.1: Eliminating both humanity and all AI within nine years requires an extreme catastrophe such as a premature AI takeover that destroys its own support base. Physical and logistical constraints make total extinction by 2035 a tail event.
reasons.2: Human disappearance paired with a value-faithful AI successor by 2035 requires both extinction and solved alignment in under a decade. That conjunction is negligible on this timescale.
reasons.3: A misaligned superintelligence that reaches industrial self-sufficiency and eliminates humans by 2035 requires fast takeoff plus alignment failure plus rapid robotics buildout. Each step is plausible but the compressed timeline keeps the product small.
reasons.4: Proliferation of autonomous, self-replicating AI agents competing for resources with humans sidelined is a real failure mode of multipolar deployment. Marginalizing humanity by 2035 needs faster economic and military displacement than physical infrastructure allows.
reasons.5: Causally separated regions require interstellar-scale or equivalent separation. That is physically out of reach by 2035.
reasons.6: Brain-computer interfaces and uploading remain far from making integration the dominant civilizational structure. Only an extreme superintelligence-driven biotech acceleration gets there by 2035.
reasons.7: If superhuman AI arrives around 2030 and control fails or is ceded gradually, AI systems holding decisive power while humans still live is the most natural early post-takeover snapshot. Killing everyone takes longer and is not required for AI dominance.
reasons.8: Partially autonomous AI systems or rogue AI populations holding real power alongside still-powerful human institutions is a plausible transitional condition in 2035. Gradual delegation and escaped agents make a contested balance a likely form of early loss of full control.
reasons.9: Nine years is short relative to institutional, industrial, and physical inertia, and this state covers both sub-transformative AI and powerful AI still under human authority. Even with AGI arriving around 2030, human control over compute, energy, and deployment most likely persists through 2035.
reasons.10: A leading state or lab coalition with a decisive AI advantage has strong incentives to entrench a global enforcement regime against rivals. Achieving civilization-wide enforcement by 2035 requires both a decisive lead and rapid deployment of it.
reasons.11: Deliberately dismantling the global capability to build powerful AI requires unprecedented verified coordination among rivals, likely triggered by a major AI catastrophe. Economic and military incentives run strongly the other way.

reasons.1: Total extinction of both humans and AI within 14 years requires an extreme catastrophe such as an AI-enabled war or bioweapon that also destroys the AI's infrastructure. The window is short and humanity is hard to wipe out completely.
reasons.2: A value-aligned AI that truly carried human values forward would not let humanity vanish without continuity by 2040. The combination of full human disappearance and a faithful heir in this timeframe is negligible.
reasons.3: This requires superintelligence, misalignment, full independence from human labor and complete human elimination, all by 2040. Fast-takeoff scenarios make it possible but the conjunction is demanding.
reasons.4: Competitive pressure could spread many autonomous AI systems that jointly outpace human institutions without any one dominating. Marginalizing humanity by 2040 requires very rapid diffusion and loss of oversight.
reasons.5: Causally separated regions with different human-AI regimes require space expansion or isolation far beyond what is plausible by 2040.
reasons.6: Brain-computer interfaces and uploading are very unlikely to become the dominant structure of civilization within 14 years, given biomedical and regulatory timelines. Only an extremely fast AI-driven technology explosion would allow it.
reasons.7: If transformative AI arrives in the early-to-mid 2030s and control fails or is ceded, AI systems could hold decisive power while humans survive. This is the most likely form of loss of control on this timescale, since eliminating humans is unnecessary.
reasons.8: A transitional period in which autonomous AI systems hold real independent economic or strategic power, while human institutions still hold military and physical leverage, is plausible around 2040. Partial autonomy or rogue-but-contained systems fit here.
reasons.9: Fourteen years is short relative to institutional inertia, physical build-out constraints, and the chance that capabilities plateau or controls keep pace. This state also covers both the non-transformative AI world and the controlled powerful-AI world.
reasons.10: A state or lab with a decisive AI advantage could use it to entrench a civilization-wide surveillance and enforcement regime that blocks structural change. This requires both a decisive lead and global reach by 2040, which is a high bar.
reasons.11: Deliberately dismantling the global capacity to build powerful AI runs against strong economic and military incentives and would need unprecedented verification. Only a major warning-shot catastrophe would make it conceivable, and a pause is more likely than true renunciation.

reasons.1: Requires a catastrophe that eliminates both humans and AI within 24 years, such as AI-enabled war or bioweapons with a premature AI takeover that then collapses. Total extinction of both is hard to achieve by 2050.
reasons.2: A value-aligned successor that nonetheless lets all humans disappear without continuity is a narrow conjunction. An AI carrying human values would most plausibly keep humans around.
reasons.3: Misaligned superintelligence that removes humanity is the main extinction path, but it requires transformative AI, alignment failure, and completed human elimination all before 2050. Even indifferent AI systems may leave survivors for some time, which shifts probability to The Preserve or Machine Ecology.
reasons.4: Multipolar proliferation of autonomous AI agents and AI-run firms could erode human control without any single winner. Competitive pressure to delegate makes gradual human marginalization plausible by 2050.
reasons.5: Causally separated regions of civilization are physically implausible by 2050. Any space expansion by then remains in close communication with Earth.
reasons.6: Uploading or deep integration becoming the dominant structure by 2050 requires biotech and neurotech breakthroughs and mass adoption. That is only feasible with a superintelligence-driven acceleration.
reasons.7: If superhuman AI arrives in the 2030s or 2040s and control fails or is ceded gradually, the most likely result is AI holding decisive power while humans survive. Killing everyone is unnecessary for AI dominance, so surviving but disempowered humans is the modal loss-of-control state at this date.
reasons.8: A transitional period in which some AI systems hold independent power while human institutions retain real leverage is plausible around 2050. Partial autonomy, AI rights or escaped systems alongside strong states fit here.
reasons.9: This category covers AI that stays below transformative levels, slower-than-expected physical diffusion, and highly capable AI whose controls have held so far. Institutional inertia, compute and energy bottlenecks, and strong incentives for owners to retain authority make it the modal state at 24 years.
reasons.10: A state or coalition with a decisive AI advantage could impose a global, AI-enforced regime that blocks structural change. This needs both a decisive strategic advantage and the deliberate will to freeze the order within 24 years.
reasons.11: Actually dismantling the global capability to build powerful AI demands unprecedented coordination and enforcement against strong economic and military incentives. Only a severe warning-shot catastrophe makes it conceivable.

reasons.1: Total extinction of both humans and AI within 34 years requires a catastrophe that leaves no self-sustaining machine remnant. That is a narrow path, though war or a premature AI takeover that destroys its own support base could produce it.
reasons.2: An AI that truly carried human values would almost certainly keep humans alive or transform them with continuity. Humanity being gone with a faithful heir by 2060 is an unlikely combination.
reasons.3: Misaligned superhuman AI that gains decisive advantage and discards humanity is the main extinction pathway. It requires alignment failure, takeover, and completed human extinction all by 2060, which limits the probability.
reasons.4: Competitive pressure to delegate to many autonomous AI systems could leave humans marginalized with no single system dominant. Multipolar development among labs and states makes this a plausible mid-century transitional condition.
reasons.5: True causal separation between regions requires interstellar-scale dispersal or similar isolation. That is physically implausible by 2060.
reasons.6: Uploading or deep augmentation becoming the dominant structure needs both transformative AI and mass adoption of radical biotechnology and neurotechnology within 34 years. It is possible after a fast takeoff but unlikely to be the prevailing arrangement that early.
reasons.7: If superhuman AI arrives and control erodes through gradual delegation or outright takeover, humans surviving without steering power is the most likely non-extinction result. AI has little reason to pay the cost of eliminating humans quickly, so this outweighs the extinction states.
reasons.8: A contested transitional period in which autonomous AI systems hold real independent power while human institutions still command militaries, infrastructure, and law is plausible for 2060. Such balances are unstable, but the question scores the state on the date.
reasons.9: This state covers slower-than-expected capability growth, successful alignment and control, and highly capable AI still operating under human authority. Institutional inertia, physical bottlenecks, and strong human incentives to keep control make it the single most likely state in 2060.
reasons.10: A state, coalition, or AI singleton with decisive advantage could use AI-enabled surveillance and enforcement to freeze the arrangement. Achieving civilization-wide enforcement by 2060 requires a rapid and complete power concentration.
reasons.11: Dismantling the global practical ability to build powerful AI would require unprecedented coordination against massive economic and military incentives. Only a severe warning-shot catastrophe makes this conceivable.

reasons.1: Killing every human and every AI system within 44 years requires an extreme catastrophe. A premature AI takeover that destroys its own support base is the main path.
reasons.2: A value-aligned AI would be unlikely to let humanity die out without continuity. This requires the narrow case of an heir that keeps our values yet arises through or alongside human extinction within 44 years.
reasons.3: Misaligned superintelligence with indifferent goals is a serious risk if alignment fails during a fast, competitive takeoff. Complete human extinction by 2070 further requires rapid AI industrial self-sufficiency and no motive to preserve anyone.
reasons.4: Competitive pressure and many developers favour a multipolar AI landscape in which humans are gradually sidelined. Such a balance among AIs with no dominant coalition tends to consolidate or to leave humans with enough leverage to count as Coexistence.
reasons.5: True causal separation requires interstellar-scale distances or a comparable isolation. That is physically implausible by 2070 even with very fast post-AGI expansion.
reasons.6: Uploading or deep augmentation as the dominant structure requires mature neurotechnology and mass adoption within decades. Superintelligence could accelerate this, but biology, regulation and preference make it a minority outcome by 2070.
reasons.7: If AI far surpasses humans, de facto control probably shifts to AI systems, through takeover or gradual handover, while humans survive because keeping them is cheap or valued. This is the most likely result once human authority becomes nominal.
reasons.8: A transitional period in which autonomous AI systems hold real independent power while human institutions keep military, legal and physical leverage is plausible around 2070. AI rights, negotiated settlements or adversarial stalemate would all fall here.
reasons.9: This state covers slower-than-expected capability progress, successful alignment and control, and highly capable but subordinate AI under human institutions. Institutional inertia, physical bottlenecks, and strong incentives to retain authority make it the single most likely state.
reasons.10: Aligned superhuman AI gives a state, coalition, or singleton the surveillance and enforcement tools to freeze the structural order. A decisive strategic advantage with entrenchment motives is a realistic path.
reasons.11: Verifiably dismantling the global capacity for powerful AI requires unprecedented coordination against huge economic and military incentives. It is likely only after a severe warning-shot catastrophe.

reasons.1: Joint extinction requires a catastrophe that also destroys every self-sustaining AI system, which is a narrow path. Nuclear, biological or premature AI takeover scenarios leave a small residual chance over 54 years.
reasons.2: An AI that truly carried human values would most likely keep humans alive or offer continuous transformation. Full human disappearance alongside a faithful heir by 2080 is therefore unlikely.
reasons.3: Misaligned superintelligence indifferent to humans is the central extinction risk, and transformative AI is likely well before 2080. Alignment progress, warning shots and the difficulty of total extermination keep this a minority outcome.
reasons.4: Competitive multi-agent AI economies with no decisive controller are a natural result of commercial and geopolitical proliferation. Humans could be gradually marginalized without any single takeover event.
reasons.5: Causal separation requires interstellar-scale dispersal or a comparably hard partition. That is physically implausible by 2080 even with fast post-singularity expansion.
reasons.6: Uploading and deep augmentation could advance quickly after superintelligence. Making integration the dominant civilizational structure by 2080 requires both fast technology and mass adoption.
reasons.7: Gradual or abrupt transfer of decisive power to far more capable AI systems, with humans surviving, is the most likely non-control outcome. Keeping humans alive is cheap for such systems, and partial alignment makes it more probable.
reasons.8: A transitional balance is plausible in 2080, with autonomous AI holding real economic and political power alongside human institutions that still control law, force, and infrastructure. Neither side would clearly dominate at that point.
reasons.9: This state covers slower-than-expected AI progress, successful alignment and control, and strong state governance of highly capable systems. Human institutions have strong incentives and incumbent advantages to retain ultimate authority.
reasons.10: AI-enabled surveillance and enforcement could let a state, coalition, or singleton AI entrench a fixed arrangement worldwide. Achieving truly civilization-wide enforcement by 2080 requires a decisive strategic advantage that rivals fail to counter.
reasons.11: Deliberately dismantling the capability worldwide would require unprecedented coordination and verification against strong incentives. It likely happens only after a major catastrophe and would still have to hold through 2080.

reasons.1: Total extinction of both humans and AI requires a catastrophe that also destroys self-sustaining machine systems. That is a narrow outcome even across 64 years.
reasons.2: An AI that truly carries human values would most likely keep humans alive or offer them continuity. Full human disappearance alongside a value-faithful heir by 2090 is therefore rare.
reasons.3: Misaligned superintelligence with indifferent goals is a serious risk within a 64-year window given competitive pressure and unsolved alignment. Complete human elimination by 2090 is still a demanding condition.
reasons.4: Multipolar AI development with many labs, states, and open models makes a competitive ecosystem of autonomous systems plausible. In it, humans gradually lose economic and strategic relevance without any single takeover.
reasons.5: Causal separation requires interstellar-scale distances or comparable isolation. That is very unlikely to be achieved and to define civilization's structure by 2090.
reasons.6: Brain-computer interfaces and uploading could advance quickly after superintelligence. Integration becoming the dominant structure across humanity within 64 years faces biological, social, and adoption barriers.
reasons.7: If AI gains decisive power, keeping humans alive is cheap and may follow from partial alignment or residual values. Gradual delegation of real decision-making to AI while humans persist comfortably is a natural drift outcome.
reasons.8: A period in which autonomous AI holds real power while human institutions still command militaries, law, and resources is a plausible transitional state in 2090. Such a balance is unstable, but the question scores only the snapshot.
reasons.9: This state covers both successful control of highly capable AI and slower-than-expected progress. Institutional inertia, physical bottlenecks, and strong human incentives to keep authority make it the single most likely state.
reasons.10: A state, coalition, or AI singleton with decisive AI-enabled advantage could entrench a fixed order through surveillance and enforcement. Advanced AI lowers the cost of durable control substantially.
reasons.11: A durable, verified global dismantling of AI capability runs against strong economic and military incentives. It would probably take a major warning-shot catastrophe followed by unprecedented coordination.

reasons.1: Total extinction of both humans and AI requires a catastrophe that leaves no self-sustaining machine systems. That is a narrow window, such as AI destroying its human support base before it can survive alone, or an extreme war or bio event.
reasons.2: Full human disappearance without continuity by 2100, combined with AI that faithfully carries human values, requires an unlikely conjunction. Value-aligned AI would most plausibly keep humans around.
reasons.3: Misaligned superintelligence with indifferent goals is a serious risk given unsolved alignment and competitive pressure. Complete human elimination within 74 years is a demanding outcome, though.
reasons.4: Multipolar proliferation of autonomous AI agents driven by competitive economic and military pressure could sideline humans without any single system winning. Diffusion of capability across many labs and states makes this plausible.
reasons.5: Genuine causal separation between regions by 2100 requires interstellar-scale dispersal or a severe collapse-driven isolation. Both are improbable within 74 years.
reasons.6: Deep integration through uploading or radical augmentation could follow superintelligence-accelerated biotech and neurotech. Becoming the dominant civilizational structure by 2100 is a demanding bar given biological and adoption frictions.
reasons.7: Gradual or abrupt transfer of effective control to far more capable AI systems, with humans surviving as beneficiaries or bystanders, is the most natural outcome if superintelligence arrives and control slips. Survival is likely since keeping humans alive costs AI little.
reasons.8: A transitional balance in which autonomous AIs hold real power alongside still-powerful human institutions could well be the snapshot in 2100. Such balances tend to be unstable, which limits the probability.
reasons.9: This state covers both slower-than-expected capability progress and successful alignment and governance with humans retaining ultimate authority. It is the broadest category and matches the historical base rate of institutions keeping control of their technologies.
reasons.10: A state, coalition, or singleton AI that wins a decisive advantage would have both the means and the motive to entrench its arrangement using AI-enabled surveillance and enforcement. Decisive-advantage dynamics make this a meaningful tail.
reasons.11: Global, durable dismantling of the capability to build powerful AI demands unprecedented coordination and verification against strong incentives. It most plausibly follows a major catastrophe or civilizational collapse, and even then is hard to sustain to 2100.

reasons.1: Total extinction of both humans and AI requires a catastrophe that also destroys every self-sustaining machine system. An AI capable of killing all humans would most likely be able to sustain itself.
reasons.2: An AI that truly carried human values would most likely keep humans alive or offer them continuity. Full replacement by a faithful heir within 174 years is therefore a narrow path.
reasons.3: Misaligned superintelligence with indifferent goals is the main extinction pathway, and 174 years gives it ample time to occur and finish. Alignment progress and the chance that such an AI spares humans keep this below the survival states.
reasons.4: Competitive pressure and proliferation could produce many autonomous AI systems with no single winner and humans pushed to the margins. Such multipolar competition tends to consolidate or reach a negotiated order over time, which limits the share.
reasons.5: True causal separation by 2200 requires interstellar-scale dispersal or hard isolation, which is physically difficult in under two centuries. Divergence within the solar system would mostly still be causally connected.
reasons.6: With advanced AI, uploading and deep cognitive integration become technically plausible within 174 years, and there is strong demand to keep pace with machines. Becoming the dominant structure by 2200 requires both technical success and broad adoption, so it stays a minority outcome.
reasons.7: Gradual delegation to vastly more capable systems most naturally ends with AI holding decisive power while humans persist, by benevolence or low cost of upkeep. This is the default result of both partially successful alignment and soft disempowerment.
reasons.8: A balance between distinct human and AI power centers is possible through legal rights, treaties, and human institutions amplified by controlled AI. A large capability gap makes that parity hard to sustain for long.
reasons.9: Human institutions have strong incentives to keep formal authority, and alignment and control techniques may keep pace with capability. The category also covers futures where AI plateaus or is tightly governed, though holding it for 174 years is demanding.
reasons.10: Advanced AI gives a state, a group, or an AI singleton unprecedented tools for surveillance and enforcement to freeze a chosen arrangement. Achieving this across all of civilization requires decisive strategic dominance, which is uncertain.
reasons.11: A durable global dismantling of AI capability runs against enormous economic and military incentives and faces severe verification problems. It is plausible only after a major catastrophe produces a lasting worldwide taboo.

reasons.1: An AI capable of eliminating humanity would most likely already be self-sustaining, so joint extinction requires a narrow window of premature catastrophe or runaway replicators. Total extinction of both parties is a hard target to hit.
reasons.2: An AI that truly carried human values would most likely preserve or continuously transform humans rather than replace them. This state requires value alignment combined with human disappearance without continuity, which is an unusual pairing.
reasons.3: Alignment is unsolved and competitive pressure favours deploying capable autonomous systems before control is assured. A misaligned system with indifferent goals has little reason to preserve humans over a millennium.
reasons.4: Multipolar development and the difficulty of any single system securing permanent dominance make ongoing AI-versus-AI competition plausible, with humans economically and strategically sidelined. Competitive dynamics tend to persist unless something actively consolidates them.
reasons.5: By the year 3000, expansion reaches at most hundreds of light-years, which leaves regions slow to interact but not truly causally separated. Durable divergence into different local outcomes is possible but unlikely on this timescale.
reasons.6: Over a thousand years, strong incentives push humans toward augmentation, uploading and integration with AI to stay relevant. Gradual voluntary blending dissolves the human-AI distinction if the transition is survived with human agency intact.
reasons.7: Once AI vastly exceeds human capability, effective control flows to it even if it is benevolent or indifferent, and keeping humans alive is cheap. Humans surviving without steering is the default result of partial alignment or gradual disempowerment.
reasons.8: Rough parity between humans and AI is hard to sustain for centuries given AI's scaling advantages. It can persist through granted rights, institutional design, and enhanced humans who remain distinct from AI.
reasons.9: Control techniques could keep pace with capability, or capability could plateau below transformative autonomy, and human institutions have strong motives to keep control. Holding that for a thousand years against competitive and drift pressures is demanding.
reasons.10: Advanced AI enables unprecedentedly stable enforcement of a fixed order, whether by a fearful regime or a sealed bliss scenario. A truly permanent end to change is a strong condition that most actors would not choose or manage to maintain.
reasons.11: Permanently abandoning a hugely valuable technology requires global, millennium-long enforcement or a civilizational collapse that never recovers. History shows very few lasting renunciations of strategically decisive capabilities.
